0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.q: חַלְּצֵ֣⁠נִי יְ֭הוָה מֵ⁠אָדָ֣ם רָ֑ע מֵ⁠אִ֖ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵֽ⁠נִי
1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, rescue me and preserve me from evil, violent people]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please rescue me]

David is using the possessive form to describe **a man** who is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a violent man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from a man who acts violently]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please preserve me]

2.note: The word **who** refers to the evil man and the man of violence from the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these evil people devise evil things]

Here, **heart** represents a person’s thoughts and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [have devised evil things in their thoughts]

David is saying **all the day** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [constantly] or [all the time]

The phrase **travel around** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. Many translations, however, follow an alternative reading found in one Hebrew manuscript and some ancient translations. The UST follows that reading. Alternate translation: [they stir up battles]

The pronoun **they** refers to the evil man and the man of violence from verse 1. David uses the plural because he has multiple enemies in view. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these evil people stir up battles]

3.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a **serpent** has a dangerous, darting tongue, so the speech of these evil people is harmful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They use their words to harm people, as a serpent uses its tongue to strike]
Here, **their tongue** represents their speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their words]

David is speaking of the harmful words of these evil people as if the words were **venom of a viper** under their lips. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the words they speak are deadly and destructive]
Here, **their lips** represents what they say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their speech]

4.q: שָׁמְרֵ֤⁠נִי יְהוָ֨ה ׀ מִ֘⁠ידֵ֤י רָשָׁ֗ע מֵ⁠אִ֣ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵ֑⁠נִי
4.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, guard me and preserve me from wicked, violent people]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please guard me]

Here, **the hands** of the wicked represents their power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of the wicked]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

David is using the possessive form to describe **the man** who is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the violent man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the man who acts violently]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from anyone of]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please preserve me]

David is speaking of his way of life as if it were a path with **steps** that his enemies could **push down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who have planned to ruin my life]
The word **who** refers to the wicked and the man of violence. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the wicked people that have planned]

5.q: טָֽמְנֽוּ־גֵאִ֨ים ׀ פַּ֡ח לִ֗⁠י וַ⁠חֲבָלִ֗ים פָּ֣רְשׂוּ רֶ֭שֶׁת לְ⁠יַד־מַעְגָּ֑ל מֹקְשִׁ֖ים שָֽׁתוּ־לִ֣⁠י
5.note: David is speaking of his enemies as if they were hunters setting **a snare**, **cords**, **a net**, and **traps** to capture him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The proud have made secret plans to ruin me; they have plotted to catch me in their schemes wherever I go]

David is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Those who are proud] or [Those who act proudly]

6.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please give ear, Yahweh, to the voice of my supplications]
David is using the term **ear** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here, **the voice** represents the words that David speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the words of my supplications]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **supplications**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my cries for help]

7.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the mighty one who rescues me]

David is speaking of God’s ability to save him as if it were physical **strength**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you who powerfully deliver me]

David is speaking of Yahweh’s protection as if Yahweh had physically **covered** his **head** with armor in battle. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have protected me when I was in battle]

David is using **in the day of battle** as a common expression to mean “at the time of battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I was in battle] or [at the time of fighting]

8.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not grant, Yahweh, the desires of the wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desires**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the wicked wish for]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not bring forth his plot]

David is using **bring forth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “grant success to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [grant success to his plot]

The pronoun **his** is singular, even though David used the plural **the wicked** earlier in the verse. This is because he is thinking of the wicked as a group that acts with a single purpose. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [their plot]

It is difficult to know how the word translated as **they rise up** fits with the rest of the verse. The interpretation of the ULT and UST is one way. Some scholars believe that the word belongs with the first line of the next verse in which case it would start a new sentence with something like: “Those who surround me raise their heads.” Here are some other possibilities. Alternate translation: [when they rise up] or [or they will rise up]

9.note: David is saying what he wants to happen to his enemies. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants to happen. Alternate translation: [I desire that the mischief of their lips cover them]

David is speaking of the harmful things his enemies have said as if those words could physically **cover them** like a burden. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the trouble they have caused by their words overwhelm them]
Here, **their lips** represents what they say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the mischief of their words]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mischief**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the troublesome things they have spoken]

10.note: David is saying what he wants to happen to his enemies. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants to happen. Alternate translation: [I desire that burning coals fall on them]

David is saying what he wants God to do to his enemies. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants God to do. Alternate translation: [may he cast them into fire]
The pronoun **him** most likely refers to God and **them** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [let God cast the enemies]

11.note: The expression **be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [May God not establish a man of tongue in the land]
Here, **tongue** represents slanderous speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [slanderous words]

David is using the possessive form to describe **a man** who is characterized by his **tongue**, that is, by his slanderous speech. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a man who speaks slander]

David is using the possessive form to describe **a man** who is characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a violent man]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a man who acts violently]

David speaks of **evil** as if it were a living thing that could **hunt** a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let him experience one disaster after another]

12.q: יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה יְ֭הוָה דִּ֣ין עָנִ֑י מִ֝שְׁפַּ֗ט אֶבְיֹנִֽים
12.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [will defend poor and needy people and bring them justice]

12.q: יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה יְ֭הוָה דִּ֣ין עָנִ֑י מִ֝שְׁפַּ֗ט אֶבְיֹנִֽים
12.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **cause** and **justice**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will defend the poor and judge fairly for the needy]

David is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. He does the same thing with the word **needy** later in the verse. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are poor]

13.q: צַ֭דִּיקִים יוֹד֣וּ לִ⁠שְׁמֶ֑⁠ךָ יֵשְׁב֥וּ יְ֝שָׁרִ֗ים אֶת־פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ
13.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [righteous and upright people will give you thanks and live in your presence]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. He does the same thing with the word **upright** later in the verse. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are righteous]
David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will thank you]

Here, **your face** represents Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the upright will live before you]
